meta.goal: Cross the line strong, smiling, and in one piece. Not a time goal — a feel-good goal.
meta.baseline: Swim is already at race distance. The bike is the biggest gap by far. The run has real fitness underneath it but very little recent volume and no half in years — so it gets built deliberately too, with run/walk from week one.
meta.race_effort: Swim easy Z2 · Bike steady Z2 all day, never once feel heroic · Run Z2 with a walk-every-aid-station plan from mile 1.

guide.start_here: This plan has one organizing idea: your swim is already done, so almost every new hour of training goes into the bike — with the run rebuilt carefully alongside it rather than assumed. That's why Saturday is sacred. Five days are mandatory (Tue, Wed, Thu, Sat, Sun) and the listed weekly hours count only those; Monday and Friday are genuinely optional extras. If a week gets messy, protect the Saturday long ride first, the Sunday long run second, and let anything else go.
guide.bike: The bike is 56 of the 70.3 miles and it's where the race is won or lost for a first-timer. You're going from ~10 mi/week to a 50-mile rehearsal ride in seven weeks, which is a real jump — so we grow the long ride by about 6 miles a week and cut it hard on step-back weeks. Three things matter more than fitness: (1) Contact points. Saddle soreness ends more first 70.3s than legs do — get properly fitted shorts, use chamois cream from week one, and if anything goes numb, stop and adjust the fit. (2) Cadence. Spin 85–90 rpm in an easy gear rather than grinding — it saves your legs for the run. (3) Never ride hard. On race day the bike should feel almost boring. Boring bike, good run.
guide.swim: Genuinely: you're already there. 2,075 yd at 1:59/100 is race distance at race pace. So the pool work here is maintenance, not building — one or two swims a week is plenty. What actually needs work is open water. Pool-fit swimmers get rattled by cold, chop, no lane line, and dozens of arms. That's why Week 4 and Week 7 both put you in a lake in a wetsuit: practice sighting every 6–8 strokes, practice starting slow and settling, and practice the dizzy jog out of the water into T1. Do those two sessions and the swim will be the easiest leg of your day.
guide.run: You have real running fitness — 7.7 miles at 9:31/mi proves it — but you haven't raced a half in years and your last four weeks averaged about 7.7 miles across two runs. Real fitness, thin recent volume. So the run gets built deliberately, and three choices make that safe. (1) Frequency over distance: we go from two runs a week to three, but the longest run in Week 1 is FIVE miles — shorter than the one you just did. More often, less far, is how durability actually gets built, and it's what protects your knees and shins while bike volume is climbing at the same time. (2) Run/walk from day one: every long run is run 9 minutes / walk 1 minute starting in Week 1 — not as a fallback when you're tired, as the method. It's exactly what you'll do on race day, so we rehearse it for nine weeks instead of improvising it at mile 3. (3) Almost no run intensity: there are no tempo runs in this plan at all. Every hard interval lives on the bike, which is non-impact and is where you actually need the fitness. Runs are easy, plus a few relaxed strides. The long run peaks at 9 miles in Week 6 and that is genuinely enough — you do not need to run 13 in training to run/walk 13 on race day, and the Week 7 brick off a 50-mile ride will teach you more about race day than any standalone long run could.
guide.bricks: A brick is a run immediately off the bike. The first 8–10 minutes your legs feel like someone else's — heavy, wobbly, oddly slow. That feeling is completely normal and it passes. The only way to stop being surprised by it is to have felt it six times before race day, which is exactly what the Saturday brick jogs are for. Keep them short and easy; they're a nervous-system rehearsal, not a workout.
guide.fuel: Anything over about 90 minutes needs calories going in. Target 200–250 cal/hr and roughly one bottle of fluid per hour on the bike, taken on a timer — not when you feel like it, because by then it's late. Practice the exact products on the Week 3, 5, 6 and 7 long rides so race day contains zero new foods. On the run, take something at most aid stations and drink even when you don't want to. The #1 cause of a miserable back half is under-fueling on the bike.
guide.gear: Before Week 6, have these sorted: a bike that fits and has been tuned, a spare tube + tire lever + a way to inflate it (and one practice run at changing a flat), a wetsuit you've actually swum in, tri shorts or shorts you've ridden 3+ hours in, chamois cream, sunglasses, and race-day nutrition you've tested. Nothing new on race day — not shoes, not gels, not a shirt.
guide.strength: Friday's optional session is knee and hip insurance, not bodybuilding. 30 minutes: glute bridges, Bulgarian split squats, step-downs, calf raises, side planks, bird dogs. Two rounds. It's the first thing to drop when the week gets busy — but if you can keep it, your hips will thank you around mile 40 of the bike.
guide.race_day_math: Rough, honest estimate at your current fitness: swim ~50–55 min · T1 ~8 min · bike 56 mi at 13 mph ~4:20 · T2 ~5 min · run 13.1 as run/walk at ~13:00/mi ~2:50. Total around 8:00–8:15. If the bike comes up to 15 mph over the next nine weeks — very possible from this starting point — that drops to roughly 7:30. IMPORTANT: check the official race bike cutoff and overall cutoff against these numbers before you commit. If the margin looks thin, the Olympic distance on the same day is a fantastic race and not a downgrade.
guide.race_day_pacing: Swim: start at the back or the side, go out embarrassingly easy for 200 yards, then settle. Bike: hold an effort you could hold for another hour after you finish. If you're passing lots of people in the first 20 miles, you're going too hard. Eat and drink on schedule. Run: run 9 / walk 1 from the very first mile. Walk every aid station, drink something at each one, and let yourself be slow. Slow and steady finishes strong — fast and clever finishes at the medical tent.
guide.listening: Back off, without guilt, if you get: resting heart rate up 7+ beats for two mornings, sleep going sideways, a joint pain that changes how you move (as opposed to general muscle soreness), or a genuine loss of enthusiasm for training. Pay extra attention to shins, knees and Achilles in the first three weeks — that's when run frequency is climbing fastest and it's the most likely place for something to grumble. The fix is almost always one or two easy days, not pushing through. Missing one session costs nothing. Missing three weeks to an injury costs the race.
guide.adjusting: Life happens — move days around freely, with two rules. Keep the long ride and long run on separate days, and never stack two hard days back-to-back. If you miss the Saturday ride, do it Sunday and shift the long run to Monday rather than skipping it. If you miss a whole week, don't try to catch up — repeat the week you missed and pull one week off the end of the build. The plan bends. That's what it's for.
